<u>**In detail**:</u>
Suppose we have $n$ tumor samples and each of them is analyzed by $m$ different types of techniques generating $m$ sets of genomic data. For example, microarray-based platforms can generate continuous data for gene expression, DNA copy number and CpG site methylation, while sequencing-based platforms can generate count data for gene expression and binary data for DNA mutation.
<ol>
  <li>Let $y_{it} = (y_{i1t}, \ldots, y_{ip_{t}t})^T$ denote a $p_t-$dimensional vector. Each element $y_{ijt}$ denotes the observed data associated with the $j-$th genomic feature in the $i-$th $(i \in \{1, \ldots n\})$ sample of the $t-$th $(t \in \{1, \ldots, m\})$ data type.</li>
  <li>The $t-$th dataset can be represented by $Y_t = (y_{1t}, \ldots, y_{nt})$, a matrix with dimensions $p_t \times n$, and all the datasets can be represented by a multi-high dimensional genomic data space $\{Y_t\}^m_{t=1}$.</li>
  <li>Assume there are $k+1, \quad (k>0)$ molecular subtypes in the tumor samples and we hope to identify them from the multi-high dimensional data space $\{Y_t\}^m_{t=1}$. The core idea is to reduce the multi-high dimensional data space to a low dimensional subspace that will collectively capture the major variations of the multiple genomic datasets. The low dimensional subspace can then be used to cluster the tumor samples.
  
  Borrowing the idea from PCA, we assume that we could project the multi-high dimensional space $\{Y_t\}^m_{t=1}$ to a low dimensional integrated subspace $Z$ with dimensions $n \times k$. In other words, each sample is associated with a latent variable $z_i = (z_{i1}, \ldots, z_{ik}), \quad i \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$, where $z_i$ is a continuous variable and follows a standard multivariate normal distribution $\textbf{MVN}(0, \textbf{I}_k)$.</li>
  <li>
    <ul>
      <li><b>Omics with continuous measurements</b>
      $$y_{ijt} = \textbf{x}_i\boldsymbol{\Gamma}
_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt} + \epsilon_{ijt}, \quad i = 1, \ldots, n, \quad j = 1, \ldots, p_t, \quad t \in (1, \ldots, m)$$
      where $\boldsymbol{\beta_{jt}} = (\beta_{0jt}, \beta_{1jt}, \ldots, \beta_{kjt})^T$ is the coefficient vector associated with the $j-$th feature in the $t-$th dataset, $\textbf{x}_i = (1, z_i) = (1, z_{i1}, \ldots, z_{ik})$ is a vector in which the first component is 1 and all the remaining components are exactly from vector $z_i$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt} = \text{diag}(1, \gamma_{jt}, \ldots, \gamma_{jt})$ is a diagonal matrix whose first diagonal component is 1 and the all the remaining $k$ diagonal components are $\gamma_{jt}$, and $\epsilon_{ijt}$ is the random error with mean 0 and variance $\sigma_{jt}^2$.</li>
      <li>The constant 1 in $\textbf{x}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}$ is designed to let the model have the intercept $\b_{0jt}$. In the model, $\gamma_{jt}$ is an indicator variable with value 0 (indicates that the corresponding $\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}$ is small and thus the $j-$th omics feature in the $t-$th dataset contributes little for joint clustering) or 1 (indicates that the corresponding $\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}$ is small and thus the $j-$th omics features in the $t-$th dataset is a contributor for the joint clustering, which is used for Bayesian variable selection).</li>
      <li>Let $y_{jt} = (y_{1jt}, \ldots, y_{njt})^T$ be the data vector of omics feature $j$ for samples $1 \ldots n$. Let $\textbf{X} = (\textbf{x}_1, \ldots, \textbf{x}_n)^T$ be the design matrix with dimensions $n \times (k+1)$, where row $i$ is $\textbf{x}_i$. Then, the model for omics feature $j$ in dataset $t$ can be written as:
      $$y_{jt} = \textbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{jt}, \quad j = 1, \ldots, p_t, \quad t \in (1, \ldots, m)$$
      where $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{jt} = (\epsilon_{1jt}, \epsilon_{2jt}, \ldots, \epsilon_{njt})^T$.</li>
      <li>To perform Bayesian analysis, we assume the following priors for the model parameters:
      $$\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt} \sim \text{MVN}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0t}, \Sigma_{0t}), \quad \sigma_{jt}^2 \sim \text{IG}(\frac{\nu_0}{2}, \frac{\nu_0 \sigma_0^2}{2}), \quad \gamma_{jt} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(q_t)$$
      In other words, we assume that the coefficient vector $\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}$ follows a multivariate normal distribution with mean $\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0t}$ and covariance $\Sigma_{0t}$; $\sigma_{jt}^2$ follows an inverse-gamma distribution with shape parameter $\frac{\nu_0}{2}$ and scale parameter $\frac{\nu_0 \sigma_0^2}{2}$; indicator variable $\gamma_{jt}$ follows a Bernoulli distribution with probability of an omics feature being selected as a driving factor for clustering being $q_t$</li>
      <li> With these assumptions, we can derive the posterior distributions of the model parameters $\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}$, $\sigma_{jt}^2$ and $\gamma_{jt}$:
      $$P(\sigma_{jt}^2 | y_{jt}, Z, \gamma_{jt}, \boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}) \sim IG(\frac{\nu_0 + n}{2}, \frac{\nu_0\sigma_0^2 + (y_jt- \textbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt})^T(y_jt- \textbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt})}{2})$$
      $$P(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt} | y_{jt}, Z, \sigma_{jt}^2, \gamma_{jt}) \sim \text{MVN}(\textbf{m, V}) \\
      \textbf{m} = (\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}^T\textbf{X}^T\textbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}/\sigma_{jt}^2 + \Sigma_{0t}^{-1})^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}^T\textbf{X}^T\textbf{X}_{jt}/\sigma_{jt}^2 + \Sigma_{0t}^{-1}\beta_{0t}) \\
      \textbf{V} = (\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}^T\textbf{X}^T\textbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}/\sigma_{jt}^2 + \Sigma_{0t}^{-1})^{-1}$$
      $$P(\gamma_{jt} | y_{jt}, Z, \boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}, \sigma_{jt}^2) \propto \exp \bigl( - \frac{(y_jt- \textbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt})^T(y_jt- \textbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt})}{2\sigma_{jt}^2}\bigr)P(\gamma_{jt})$$
      where $P(\gamma_{jt})$ is the prior of $\gamma_{jt}$. In other words, the posterior of $\sigma_{jt}^2$ is an inverse gamma distribution with scale parameter $\nu_0\sigma_0^2 + (y_jt- \textbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt})^T(y_jt- \textbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt})$ and shape parameter $(\nu_0 + n)/2$; the posterior of $\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}$ is a multivariate normal with mean $\textbf{m}$ and covariance $\textbf{V}$.</li>
      <li>Since the posteriors are known, the Gibbs sampling algorithm is used to obtain samples from the posteriors. There is no closed form for parameter $\gamma_{jt}$, but the distribution is proportional to the terms specified in the last equation. Therefore, the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm can be used to sample from its posterior. There is no closed form for $z_i$ either. The sampling strategy for $z_i$ is described later below. The idea in the end will be that the latent variable $z_i$ will be used for sample clustering and omics features with high posterior probability of $\gamma_{jt}$ being 1 will be selected as informative features.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>
    <ul>
      <li><b>Omics with binary measurements</b>
      If $y_{ijt}$ is a binary variable (e.g. mutation/no mutation) the data is modelled with classical logistic regression:
      $$\log\frac{P(y_{ijt}=1|z_i)}{1 - P(y_{ijt}=1|z_i)} = \textbf{x}_i\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}, \quad i = 1, \ldots, n, \quad j = 1, \ldots, p_t, \quad t \in (1, \ldots, m)$$
      where $P(y_{ijt}=1|z_i)$  is the probability of gene $j$ being mutant in sample $i$ given the value of the latent variable $z_i$; $\textbf{x}_i = (1, z_i)$ is the same design vector as previously, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}$ and $\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}$ have the same components as previously and data type $t$ refers to binary.</li>
      <li>Assuming that the priors for the model parameters are:
      $$\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt} \sim \text{MVN}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0t}, \Sigma_{0t}), \quad \gamma_{jt} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(q_t)$$
      the posteriors then are:
      $$P(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt} | y_{jt}, Z, \gamma_{jt}) \propto \bigl(\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{(\exp(\textbf{x}_i\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}))^{y_{ijt}}}{1 + \exp(\textbf{x}_i\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt})}\bigr) \exp \bigl(-\frac{1}{2} (\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt} - \boldsymbol{\beta}_{0t})^T\Sigma_{0t}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt} - \boldsymbol{\beta}_{0t})\bigr) \\
      P(\gamma_{jt} | y_{jt}, Z, \boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}) \propto \bigl(\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{(\exp(\textbf{x}_i\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}))^{y_{ijt}}}{1 + \exp(\textbf{x}_i\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt})}\bigr) P(\gamma_{jt})$$</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>
    <ul>
      <li><b>Omics with count measurements</b>
      When $y_{ijt}$ is a count variable (e.g. RNA-seq data), the data is modelled using Poisson regression:
      $$\log(\lambda(y_{ijt} | z_i)) = \textbf{x}_i\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}, \quad i = 1, \ldots, n, \quad j = 1, \ldots, p_t, t \in (1, \ldots, m)$$
      where $\lambda(y_{ijt} | z_i)$ is the predicted mean of $y_{ijt}$ conditional on the latent variable $z_i$; $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}$ and $\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}$ are the corresponding indicator variable and parameter for the count data type (simlar to those in the continuous and binary cases).</li>
      <li>Assuming that the priors for the model parameters are:
      $$\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt} \sim \text{MVN}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0t}, \Sigma_{0t}), \quad \gamma_{jt} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(q_t)$$
      the posteriors then are:
      $$P(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt} | y_{jt}, Z, \gamma_{jt}) \propto \bigl(\prod_{i=1}^n(\exp(\textbf{x}_i\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}))^{y_{ijt}}\exp(-\exp(\textbf{x}_i\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}))\bigr)\exp\bigl(-\frac{1}{2} (\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt} - \boldsymbol{\beta}_{0t})^T\Sigma_{0t}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt} - \boldsymbol{\beta}_{0t})\bigr) \\
      P(\gamma_{jt} | y_{jt}, Z, \boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}) \propto \bigl(\prod_{i=1}^n(\exp(\textbf{x}_i\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}))^{y_{ijt}}\exp(-\exp(\textbf{x}_i\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}))\bigr)P(\gamma_{jt})$$
      </li>
      <li>The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm is used to jointly sample $(\gamma_{jt}, \boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt})$ from their posteriors.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>Now, let sample $i$ be associated with latent variable $z_i$. Through joint modelling, $z_i$ will collectively capture the major biological variations across the omics data of the cancer samples and provide a basis for predicting if an omics feature $j$ in a given dataset $t$ is a driver for sample clustering. The joint model can be written as:
  $$P(y_{ijt}, z_i | \boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}, \gamma_{jt}, i=1,\ldots,n, j=1,\ldots,p_t, t=1,\ldots,m) = \prod_{t}^m \prod_{i}^n \prod_{j}^{p_t} P(y_{ijt} | z_i, \boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}, \gamma_{jt})P(z_i)$$
  where the multiplication is due to the conditional independence assumption of $y_{ijt}$ given $z_i$; $P(z_i)$ is the density function of the standard $\text{MVN}(\textbf{0,I}_k)$; the conditional density function $P(y_{ijt} | z_i, \boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}, \gamma_{jt})$ has the form of normal, Bernoulli or Poisson depending on the type of omics data. More specifically,
  $$
P(y_{ijt} | z_i, \boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}, \gamma_{jt}) \propto 
  \begin{cases}
    \sigma_{jt}^{-1}\exp\left(-\frac{(y_{ijt}-\textbf{x}_i\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt})^2}{2\sigma_{jt}^2}\right), & \text{normal}, \\
    \left(\exp(\textbf{x}_i\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt})\right)^{y_{ijt}}\left(1+\exp(\textbf{x}_i\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt})\right)^{-1}, & \text{binomial}, \\
    \left(\exp(\textbf{x}_i\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt})\right)^{y_{ijt}}\exp\left(-\exp(\textbf{x}_i\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{jt}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt})\right), & \text{Poisson},
  \end{cases}
$$</li>
<li>The latent variable $z_i$ is not observable and therefore we need the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method to obtain samples from its posterior distribution for statistical inference. The exact posterior of $z_i$ is not known. However, we know it's proportional to the product of the density of $z_i$ and the joint likelihood of the data:
  $$P\left( z_i | y_{jt}, \boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}, \gamma_{jt} \right) \propto P(z_i) \prod_{t=m}^{T} \prod_{j=p_t}^{P} P\left( y_{ijt} | Z_i, \boldsymbol{\beta}_{jt}, \gamma_{jt} \right), \quad i=1, 2, \ldots, n.
$$
Therefore, the Metropolis–Hasting algorithm will be used to sample from its posterior distribution for statistical inference.</li>
  <li>The mean values of the latent variables are used for clustering. Specifically, following a general principle for separating $g$ clusters among $n$ data points, the $k-$ means algorithm is used to divide the $n$ samples into $g$ clusters in the latent variable space, where $g = k + 1$.</li>
</ol>
